item.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2573
Authors: Muhammad Imran
Summary: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/\epsilon))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}_K/N\mathcal{O}_K)$ for number fields $K$.

item.title: DISCO*: DIstributed and SCalable Oblivious Joins and Oblivious Primitives
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2572
Authors: Apostolos Mavrogiannakis, Xian Wang, Ioannis Demertzis, Dimitrios Papadopoulos, Minos Garofalakis
Summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) let clients outsource computation to untrusted clouds, but they remain vulnerable to side-channel and leakage-abuse attacks. Recent work closes this gap by combining hardware enclaves with oblivious computation, which offers strong security guarantees yet struggles to meet the performance and scalability demands of real-world deployments. In this work, we present DISCO, the first scalable, distributed, and fully oblivious database system that seamlessly combines hardware enclaves with cutting-edge oblivious primitives and novel optimizations that significantly reduce inter-server communication overheads. What distinguishes DISCO from prior work is a suite of distributed frameworks that unlock parallel computation and fundamentally shift the design paradigm of distributed oblivious systems, enabling practical deployment at scales that were unattainable with previous solutions. We provide a thorough evaluation of the performance of our system on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our evaluation demonstrates that our design significantly reduces the gap between theory and practice, achieving 88× speedup over Jodes and 180× over SODA on non-foreign key joins with N = 2²⁵ elements. Most importantly, we report, for the first time, results for computations at the terabyte scale.

item.title: A Spectral Theory of Local-to-Global Leakage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2571
Authors: Rei Ueno
Summary: This paper studies how local leakages characterize the global leakage in additive secret sharing over a finite abelian group, which is a special case of linear secret sharing and side-channel masking. Our main finding is structural: local-to-global leakage is governed by two disjoint components---the magnitude of local leakage and its spectral alignment across shares, while existing literature attempted to characterize the global leakage only by local mutual information (MI). We first give an exact decomposition of leakage in additive secret sharing. The decomposition reveals a structural parameter invisible to MI, while previous literature conjectured that the local MI alone suffices to characterize global leakage. We then show that this missing parameter is indispensable: two leakage channels with identical local MI can induce exponentially different global leakage. Our exact decomposition identifies the missing structural quantity and completely characterizes this phenomenon.
We then show the separation theorem with its realizability---local MI, despite governing the classical leakage bounds, does not even determine the exponential rate at which leakage vanishes under homomorphic composition. More strongly, we establish a universal separation theorem: even when all permutation-invariant scalar measures of local leakage agree, the global leakage can exhibit exponentially different decay rates.
We further provide the characterization of the spectral alignment factor and derive its lower bound through character-order multiplicity and Möbius inversion. We then extend the framework to automorphism-weighted sharing. We establish that automorphism-weighted sharing can achieve perfect leakage cancellation with finitely many shares, even for non-trivial full-support local leakage channels. In sharp contrast, such perfect cancellation is impossible for ordinary additive sharing with non-trivial i.i.d local leakage channels and finitely many shares.
Consequently, local leakage magnitudes correctly measure the average amount of local leakage, but discard the compatibility structure needed for composition. Magnitude-only bounds must optimize over structural alignments that the actual leakage channel does not realize.

item.title: Membership Inference in Privacy-Preserving Vector Search
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2570
Authors: Georg Fuchsbauer, Carter Luck, Adam O'Neill, Ian Rapko
Summary: Vector retrieval increasingly runs over sensitive embedding databases. Backend-compatible protections are desirable in such settings in that they transform the plaintext vectors while leaving the search algorithm itself unchanged. However, the protected database then leaks some geometry, that is, information about the distances between the stored vectors. We study membership-inference attacks on such leakage given a single database snapshot and known plaintexts. Our central finding is that membership privacy depends on how much geometry is revealed and on whether known plaintexts can be linked to positions in the snapshot, and that the effect of each of these depends on the other.
We first break the prior Scale-and-Perturb (SAP) scheme of Fuchsbauer et al. (FGHO, SCN 2022) with no known plaintexts. Empirically, our attack achieves advantage 0.997 on MS-MARCO. We then introduce Rotate-and-Perturb (RAP), a special case of a scheme FGHO call SAP-I and leave unanalyzed. For uniform data on the sphere, we prove perfect membership privacy with no known plaintexts. For fixed noise parameter β ∈ (0, 2], achieving constant advantage requires a number of known plaintext-ciphertext pairs at least logarithmic in the database size, provided that number is below the embedding dimension. Empirically, our attack reaches advantage 0.5 with 3 such pairs at database size 100 and 7 at 100,000 on text embeddings.
We also study two more approaches, namely ideal distance-comparison-revealing encryption (DCRE) and an encrypted HNSW index using function-hiding inner-product functional encryption. Ideal DCRE remains vulnerable to known plaintext-ciphertext pairs. On the tested MS-MARCO databases, our attack on the encrypted HNSW index requires knowing 19–32% of the database and their corresponding index vertices to reach advantage 0.5.
Finally, we study augmentations to these schemes to mitigate our attacks, shuffling and secret projection. Together, they substantially increase the number of known plaintexts needed by our tested attacks on RAP and comparison-only leakage.

item.title: Optimal Proofs of Sequential Work
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2569
Authors: Krzysztof Pietrzak, Leonid Reyzin
Summary: In a proof of sequential work (PoSW), introduced by Mahmoody, Moran and Vadhan [MMV'13], a verifier can be convinced that a prover performed a computation of $T$ sequential steps. Such a proof is $(\delta, \lambda)$-sound if a malicious prover making at most $(1-\delta)T$ sequential steps can produce a valid proof only with probability $2^{-\lambda}$, even when using massive parallelism.
Besides time-lock puzzles (TLPs) and verifiable delay functions (VDFs), PoSW are one of the central primitives in timed cryptography. Unlike TLPs or VDFs, PoSW can be constructed just from hash functions, with a security proof in the random oracle model. Existing PoSW are based on graph labeling: the prover must sequentially compute a labeling of a graph of $T$ nodes, where each node's label is the hash of its parents' labels.
The [MMV'13] construction uses node-depth-robust graphs. A simple and much more efficient construction was later given by Cohen and Pietrzak [CP'18]. In the [CP'18] PoSW, getting $(\delta, \lambda)$ soundness requires transmitting $\Omega((\lambda\log T)/\delta)$ hash outputs. The underlying graph has average in-degree $\Theta(\log T)$, so labeling takes $\Theta(T\log T)$ total hash inputs.
Our first result is a lower bound: any efficient graph-labeling-based PoSW that is $(\delta, \lambda)$-sound requires the prover to send $\Omega((\lambda\log T)/\delta)$ labels. To prove this result, we relate PoSW soundness to a cut-depth game and bound this game using a refinement of Valiant's depth-reduction argument. This shows that [CP'18] achieves asymptotically optimal communication and verifier hash-input complexity, while leaving open whether its $\Theta(\log T)$ average indegree (and thus $\Theta(T\log T)$ prover hash-input complexity) is necessary.
Our second result is a new PoSW that matches these lower bounds up to constant factors and has maximum indegree two. In particular, it reduces the honest prover's total hash-input complexity from $\Theta(T\log T)$ to $\Theta(T)$ while retaining $O((\lambda\log T)/\delta)$ communication and verifier hash-input complexity.

item.title: Efficient NTRU+ Implementations on Cortex-M
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2568
Authors: Subeen Cho, Minjoo Sim, Seungwon Lee, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Wai Kong Lee, Hwajeong Seo
Summary: Post-quantum cryptography on embedded devices requires implementations that perform cryptographic operations efficiently within limited computation and memory. Most lattice-based KEMs use 2-way NTTs over power-of-two cyclotomic rings, and their embedded implementations have been studied extensively. In contrast, implementations of schemes based on 3-way NTTs, which combine radix-3 and radix-2 layers, remain scarce. This work therefore presents efficient implementations of NTRU+, a KEM built on 3-way NTTs, on Arm Cortex-M0+, M3, M4, and M7. We configure the layer fusion, modular arithmetic, and instruction scheduling of the 3-way NTT for each parameter set and core. We also introduce ω-folded front layers, which compute the first two layers of the forward NTT on ternary inputs without modular reduction. Based on these techniques, we present two implementations. The speed-optimized implementation keeps operands as full polynomial arrays to prioritize execution time. The memory-optimized implementation reuses a single polynomial workspace and regenerates the required operands in pieces aligned with radix-3 blocks. On physical boards, the speed-optimized implementation reduces execution time by up to 52.43% compared with the official optimized C implementation. The memory-optimized implementation reduces peak stack usage by up to 82.60% while running faster than the official optimized C implementation in every KEM operation. A controlled NTT-replacement experiment and per-technique comparisons show that the same technique can have different effects depending on the instruction set and pipeline of each core.

item.title: A Systematic Evaluation of Fault Attacks and Countermeasures on ML-DSA Rejection Sampling
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2567
Authors: Yulong Meng
Summary: This paper presents a systematic evaluation of fault attacks on the rejection sampling of ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and of the countermeasures proposed against them. Using the identity \(\mathbf{Az} - ct = \mathbf{Ay} - c\cdot\mathbf{s}_2 = \mathbf{r}\), we prove that the quantity compared by the "third rejection test" of patent WO2025261784A1 is exactly \(\mathbf{r}_1\), which is already produced during signing, while check 2 passing is what implies \(\mathbf{r}_1 = \mathbf{w}_1\). The third check therefore re-verifies a condition that check 2 guarantees, rather than being an independent test. We further show that the six embodiments claimed by the patent reduce to only two independent conditions, both covering only skips of the second check. An experiment with 30,000 fault injections confirms that all six embodiments detect the skip of the \(\mathbf{z}\)-norm check — the route that directly recovers the signing key \(\mathbf{s}_1\) — at a rate of zero. Building on this blind spot, we fully recover \(\mathbf{s}_1\) against a third-check-protected implementation (all 1024 coefficients of the four polynomials) under randomized signing, the default form in FIPS 204. We then report a complete evaluation matrix over three fault models and two implementation variants, and show that the third check and sign-then-verify are complementary with neither being sufficient on its own: the latter fails entirely against the second-check skip on the reference implementation (all faulty signatures pass verification), while the cheapest embodiment of the former detects every exploitable signature, whereas against the \(\mathbf{z}\)-check skip only sign-then-verify is effective. Their union covers every attack path we evaluate, and deploying either one alone leaves a complete attack path open. Overhead measurements show that this embodiment costs 0.04–0.05% of a signing on x86-64 and 0.83% on Cortex-M4, about 460–590 and 48 times less than sign-then-verify on the same platforms (22–24% and 40.0%, respectively). We therefore recommend deploying both, at a combined cost that is almost entirely sign-then-verify's.

item.title: Fault-Induced Nonce Repetition in Threshold Lattice Signatures: A Reveal-Structure Criterion, Cross-Scheme Analysis, and Detection Boundaries
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2566
Authors: Yulong Meng
Summary: Threshold ML-DSA is regarded as a deployment model that eliminates single-point key risk, and the NIST threshold call (IR 8214C) has likewise attracted many proposals. Existing security analyses, however, generally assume malicious or compromised protocol participants. For the threat of "physical faults in the devices of honest participants," single-party lattice signatures have been studied systematically for over a decade, whereas threshold schemes, to our knowledge, have not yet been systematically evaluated. We show that fault-induced cross-session sample replay by one party leaks that party's share, and that mechanisms such as RNG state rollback can trigger it. In a t-of-n deployment, the attacker need only fault t devices to recover the complete signing secret, while every signature is fully valid when examined individually; the hedged nonce, commitment/session binding, and fail-closed final verification all remain untriggered. We verify the attack end to end on Mithril (ePrint 2026/013, USENIX Security 2026): two implementation versions, six (t,n) configurations, and 96/96 statistical scan groups all achieve exact recovery, with residual error identically 0 and no lattice reduction. The secret recovered solely from the coordinator-visible transcript can be used to forge a signature on the spot that passes the implementation's FIPS 204 verifier. We further elevate the attack to a class-level criterion. The attack surface is determined by the reveal structure, that is, by whether the scheme reveals per-party responses to a party visible to the attacker, rather than by the distributional properties of the nonce. Quorus's structural immunity thus comes from non-reveal and is unrelated to uniformity. TALUS can be broken via a double-spend path in which "one-time consumption of preprocessing is skipped". Trilithium's signing algorithm hands the Server's response share to the Client in plaintext, and [TALUS] classifies it as internally uniform (\(I = 0\)), making it an instance of the "statistically immune and fault-fragile" quadrant; the attack requires only 1 device fault. The simulator message "(ss, sid, [z']_S)" in the original proof, together with [Jarv26]'s verbatim copy of this algorithm, is the evidence for this determination; see Appendix D for the evidence tier. This yields two independent evaluation dimensions: the statistical axis \(I\) and the reproducibility axis (reveal structure). Different design levers allow the two axes to take values independently. All three quadrants already have instances: (reveal, \(I > 0\)), (non-reveal, \(I = 0\)), and (reveal, \(I = 0\)). Two cases lie on the anti-diagonal, [Trilithium] and [Kao26]. We design detection as two layers of transcript-level checks. The early-warning surface alarms on reveal-hash liveness and achieves 305/305 exact hits over the full corpus with zero false positives. The full-coverage surface runs the identification computation shared with the attack; within the feasible range of identification, there is no window in which the attack is usable but undetectable. §6.1 explains the difference in alarm timing. For imperfect faults, we prove the threshold law for full-key recovery \(m^* = (\ell-1)N+\lceil N/K \rceil\) and verify it coordinate by coordinate; for ML-DSA-44 the law gives \(768+\lceil 256/K \rceil\), namely 896 at K=2 and 787 at K=14. This reveals the trade-off nature of K. All claims have undergone a tool-assisted verification workflow with three analysis paths that are independent of one another. The authors direct the workflow; §8.2 describes its execution mode and artifact disclosure.

item.title: Further Elaborations on the Provable Dual Attack
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2565
Authors: Kaveh Bashiri
Summary: The dual attack is one of the main strategies for attacking the learning-with-errors (LWE) problem. A recent line of work aims at provable analyses of dual attacks that rely on as few heuristic assumptions as possible.
We present a provable dual attack that recovers a subvector $\boldsymbol{s}_{\mathrm{guess}}$ of the LWE secret, and we derive an explicit lower bound on its success probability without any heuristic assumption. Our analysis unifies the provable approaches of Pouly and Shen (EUROCRYPT 2024) and Bashiri and Wiemers (J. Math. Cryptol. 2025), and removes the very few informal assumptions left in the previous works. Inspired by Qu, Tian, Wang, and Xu (ePrint 2026/2117), the dual vectors are sampled from the sublattice spanned by the first vectors of a reduced basis. Our key ingredient is a first-moment estimate for the wrong candidates, which is based on the exact uniform distribution of some appearing cosets. This leads us to discard certain typical assumptions on shortest vectors from previous works.
We apply our results to ML-KEM, under one heuristic on its structured matrix, and improve on the first provable dual attack by $22$ to $52$ bits without any assumption on the rank of the sublattice, and by $47$ to $100$ bits ($21$ to $56$ bits compared with Qu, Tian, Wang, and Xu (ePrint 2026/2117)) if this rank is bounded as in Qu, Tian, Wang, and Xu (ePrint 2026/2117). We also apply our results to ML-DSA, and demonstrate the attack experimentally on small instances.
Our results do not threaten the security of ML-KEM or ML-DSA.

item.title: Regular Syndrome Decoding Is Easier Than Previously Estimated
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2563
Authors: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Changmin Lee, Hochang Lee
Summary: The Regular Syndrome Decoding (RSD) problem is a structured variant of classical Syndrome Decoding and underlies a growing number of efficient cryptographic constructions, including zero-knowledge protocols, pseudorandom correlation generators, and MPC-in-the-Head signatures. Although RSD is generally believed to be computationally hard, recent works have shown that algebraic attacks can outperform information-set decoding on important RSD parameter regimes.
Building on this line of work, we revisit the concrete hardness of RSD and show that many widely used parameter sets are substantially easier to solve than previously estimated. This improvement stems from a refined hybrid-algebraic attack that exposes and removes a previously overlooked source of concrete complexity: the joint blockwise placement of zero-coordinate guesses and syndrome-based variable eliminations. Rather than treating the two guessing stages and linear elimination as largely separate choices, our method coordinates them across all regular blocks so that the guessing penalty is balanced while sufficient equations are retained for linearization. This gives a systematic block-balancing principle for the entire guess–reduce–solve pipeline.
We reassess several RSD-based applications, including Ferret (CCS~2020), Wolverine (IEEE S\&P~2021), and committed VOLE (CCS~2025). Our estimates place at least one parameter set per application below its 128-bit target, with losses approaching 67~bits. On PCG benchmarks, we improve previous best attack costs by up to 29.77 and 25.91~bits over non-binary and binary fields, respectively. Moreover, for the revised 128-bit PCG parameter sets of Liu et al. (EUROCRYPT~2024) evaluated here, estimated attack costs are all below $2^{111}$ field operations. These results substantially revise the concrete-security landscape of RSD and indicate that several existing parameter choices overestimate the hardness of their underlying RSD instances.

item.title: A New Approach to Reducing Modulus Requirements in Homomorphic Computation: Precision Allocation in CKKS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2562
Authors: Zhaoyang Liang, Runkun Liu, Jingwei Fang, Dan Ding
Summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation over encrypted data subject to the prescribed security and precision requirements (allowable deviations from ideal results). Among all FHE schemes, CKKS is a representative scheme for approximate arithmetic, allowing the same operation on multiple values packed into a single RLWE ciphertext.
Reducing ciphertext modulus \(Q\) for given output precision requirements under RLWE security constraints is a central challenge in homomorphic computation. However, despite advances in plaintext and ciphertext representations, algorithmic optimizations, and modulus management, the budget in most existing approaches remains dependent on the highest required precision and cannot reduce the baseline modulus cost to overcome encryption noise.
In this work, we make average rather than maximum precision requirements govern the modulus budget and achieve savings in the baseline cost. Under decryption correctness constraints, we make these possible by allocating arbitrary output precision among independent values and quantify the modulus savings arising from differences in their precision requirements.
As a bonus, our construction preserves the standard CKKS ciphertext format, which helps maintain compatibility with existing optimizations. And the construction inherits the IND-CPA security of CKKS without additional cryptographic assumptions.
With a 64-bit average precision requirement, we transfer 75 bits of precision without reducing evaluation depth and up to 735 bits while preserving correct initial recovery, raising the precision allocated to the target values to 2,269 bits. For six successive squarings of 256 messages targeting 224-bit precision, our implementation reduces the initial modulus bit length by 67\% compared with standard CKKS, allowing a fourfold reduction in ring dimension.

item.title: SALUS: Large-Scale Homomorphic Circuit Synthesis via Logic-Aware LUT Optimization
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2561
Authors: Ran Mao, Zhou Zhang, Zian Zhao, Zhenyu Guan, Peng Yin, Song Bian
Summary: Recently, growing interests are developed in optimizing fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) circuits to enable Boolean function evaluations over ciphertexts. While existing works utilize functional bootstrapping (FBS) to efficiently evaluate logic gates, the evaluation efficiency for large-scale circuits remains limited. Recent advances introduce a fast ciphertext conversion method, making it feasible to evaluate look-up tables (LUTs) over homomorphic multiplexer operation. In this work, we propose a new circuit synthesis framework, SALUS, which automatically generates and evaluates gate-level graphs over homomorphic LUTs given an input Boolean circuit. We apply the binary decision diagram (BDD) reordering method and multi-value refresh techniques to efficiently evaluate complex LUTs. Additionally, we propose a heuristic algorithm to merge LUTs in a given circuit into multi-output LUTs. In the experiments, we examine the efficiency of SALUS using a wide range of benchmark suites, including the EPFL and ISCAS benchmark circuits. We show that SALUS achieves a maximum reduction of up to 26× in computational latency compared to state-of-the-art homomorphic circuit synthesis method. Furthermore, we evaluate real-world applications, e.g., image filtering and matrix multiplication, and achieve an average speedup of 8.6× (with a maximum speedup of 24×) compared to the FBS-based method.

item.title: Graphs and cycles in curve-based collision walks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2560
Authors: Sebastiano Boscardin, Jolijn Cottaar, Monika Trimoska
Summary: In this work, we look at collision-based attacks both for elliptic curve and isogeny problems. Our main focus is on attacks in the multi-user setting, i.e., where one tries to recover all secret keys of a large set of $L$ public keys simultaneously, in a faster way than the total time required to attack each key individually. We consider three different problems: (1) the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves, (2) the isogeny pathfinding problem on supersingular $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$-curves, (3) the isogeny pathfinding problem on supersingular $\mathbb{F}_p$-curves. We first survey the existing van Oorschot and Wiener style attacks on these three problems. Then we propose versions of the pseudorandom walks that are better suited for isogeny pathfinding problems without additional restrictions. We then apply these new walks to the multi-user setting and analyse which properties we can achieve compared to the discrete logarithm case where we show that we can extract all $L$ public keys with $L$ useful collisions and without an infiltrator (a user for which we know the secret key). Specifically, for (2) we can extract $L$ public keys with approximately $L + \log(L)$ useful collisions and no infiltrator needed. Our analysis shows however that heuristic and infiltrator-aided strategies are more efficient while enjoying practically similar gains. For (3) we can extract approximately $0.75L$ public keys with $L$ useful collisions, but with an infiltrator.

item.title: FN-DSA on Arm Cortex-M55: Revisiting a Floating-Point Lattice Signature with Native FP64 and Helium
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2559
Authors: Seung-Won Lee, Min-Joo Sim, Min-Seo Kim, Hwa-Jeong Seo
Summary: FN-DSA has the shortest signatures among NIST's post-quantum signature standards, but on microcontrollers its signing is slow because the binary64 arithmetic it specifies is emulated with integer instructions. Previous speedups either change the arithmetic or the order of random sampling, so their signatures no longer match the known-answer tests (KATs) of the reference implementation, or rely on double-precision SIMD instructions that microcontrollers lack. The Arm Cortex-M55 has both a double-precision FPU and the M-Profile Vector Extension (MVE). On this core, we present the first FN-DSA implementation that, unlike these approaches, reproduces the KATs of the reference and runs in constant time, yet is faster than the reference. On MVE, we vectorize the NTTs with layer merging and the fixed-point FFT of key generation with split-word Q32 arithmetic on 32-bit lanes. On the FPU, bit-exact FP64 computes the FFT, LDL decomposition, split, merge and sampler of signing without changing any result, and exponent-normalized division turns the bit-by-bit divisions of key generation into a single VDIV.F64 with operand-independent latency. For Keccak, vectorized bit interleaving speeds up every permutation, and request-level batching processes four independent verification requests at once; SLOTHY then reschedules our MVE and Keccak assembly. Key generation, signing and verification become up to 1.23x, 1.93x and 1.30x faster than the reference on the same core, and batch verification of four signatures up to 1.75x faster. Overall, the FPU pays off where the reference emulates an operation with many integer instructions, and MVE where it already computes with integers or fixed point.

item.title: Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2557
Authors: Olivier Gillot, William J. Buchanan, Madjid G. Tehrani
Summary: With Q-day approaching, the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has begun, with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards. This paper benchmarks the three NIST-standardised PQC algorithms—FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)—across key generation, signing and verification operations, measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL 3.5, results show that ML-KEM and ML-DSA achieve energy and speed efficiency comparable to classical elliptic-curve cryptography across all tested architectures. However, SLH-DSA signing is inadvisable on constrained hardware: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware, making it impractical for resource-limited IoT deployments. These findings have direct implications for IoT security practitioners planning PQC migration.

item.title: Registered ABE via Predicate Encodings, Revisited
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2558
Authors: Junichi Tomida
Summary: Predicate encodings, proposed by Wee (TCC'14), are a simple framework that abstracts a variety of attribute-based encryption (ABE) schemes. Zhu et al. showed how to apply predicate encodings to registered ABE (Reg-ABE) using the same definition as in vanilla ABE (Asiacrypt'23). We provide a new definition of predicate encodings that is more suitable for registered ABE and allows us to obtain more efficient Reg-ABE schemes than those by Zhu et al. for predicates captured by predicate encodings. Notably, we obtain \begin{itemize} \item the first Reg-ABE scheme for (non-)zero inner product with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \item the first Reg-ABE scheme for conjunctions/disjunctions with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \item the first registered broadcast encryption scheme with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \end{itemize} under the standard $ k $-Lin assumption, where $ L $ denotes the maximum number of users. Prior to our work, Reg-ABE schemes for (non-)zero inner product, conjunctions, and disjunctions require $ O(\ell\log L) $-size ciphertexts where $ \ell $ is the vector length or the policy size, and registered broadcast encryption schemes rely on the generic group model.

item.title: Analysis of an AI based code distinguisher
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2556
Authors: Quentin Lavit, Julien Seinturier, Pascal Véron
Summary: Recently, DeepDistinguisher demonstrated the capability of transformer-like architectures to accurately distinguish Goppa codes from linear codes randomly generated, outperforming traditional distinguishers in certain settings. The purpose of our research is to examine the working mechanism of the mentioned machine learning algorithm. In particular, we explore the performance of the distinguisher using saliency maps and attention visualization techniques. We first identify a low-weight-row artifact present in the random instances used during training and show that the model partially relies on this feature. After removing this artifact, the distinguisher still achieves significant accuracy, suggesting the use of more structural properties. Inspired by the constraints induced by the minimum distance of Goppa codes, we proposed a rule based on pairwise XOR operation between the rows of the generator matrix. Our experiments have shown that the predictions made by DeepDistinguisher and XOR-based rule are highly correlated especially for high-rate codes. Furthermore, when evaluated on random matrices satisfying both the minimum distance and XOR constraints, the neural distinguisher loses most of its predictive power. This suggests that transformer-based architectures exploit general combinatorial properties of a code rather than some hidden underlying algebraic structure.

item.title: Post-quantum commutative group actions from oriented superspecial abelian varieties
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2555
Authors: Wouter Castryck, Bogdan Adrian Dina, Péter Kutas, Gioella Lorenzon
Summary: We study the cryptographic use of Shimura class group actions on superspecial principally polarized abelian varieties equipped with a CM orientation, within the context of post-quantum cryptography. Besides giving an accessible introduction to the topic, illustrated with many examples, we provide tools for representing CM orientations through higher-dimensional isogenies and for computing the Shimura class group action in the restricted effective group action model. Here, key auxiliary results are a version of Kani's lemma "with CM" and a trick that often allows to halve the ambient dimension. We also give a method for finding superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces that are oriented by a given CM order, which is extracted from an algebraic framework for studying CM orientations using the Ibukiyama-Katsura-Oort correspondence. We also analyze obstructions to transitivity of the Shimura class group action, related to the characteristic-zero notion of CM type.

item.title: Concrete LDVR Attacks with Fewer Signers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2554
Authors: Renas Bacho
Summary: We improve the concrete parameters of the attacks on the low-dimensional vector representation (LDVR) problem by Rodríguez García and Tessaro (ePrint 2026/2126), whose attack on canonical evaluation points uses $5{,}020$ signers. By combining their Chinese remainder theorem construction with a generalized birthday search over many challenges, we obtain a concrete attack with $488$ signers and $173$ corruptions over the Curve25519 scalar field. In $64$ batches of $2^{25}$ challenges, the search finds solutions for six distinct challenges. We compare the counts measured at each stage of the search with predictions from an explicit heuristic model. For adversarially chosen evaluation points, we build on the binary attacks of Rodríguez García and Tessaro and give a construction that attains the optimal LDVR success probability for every oracle query budget when $2\le n\le253$ and $t_c=t$ in the uniform oracle model. At $228$ signers and $114$ corruptions, our implementation finds a successful subset using SHA-512 challenges after a cumulative total of $360.13$ million queries across two runs, taking $168.60$ seconds in total. We also give an explicit set of $256$ evaluation points for which an efficient subset search attack using $128$ corruptions succeeds with probability at least $51.92\%$ per uniform challenge. For both canonical and adversarially chosen evaluation points, we analyze the query complexity and report measured and estimated running times.

item.title: Near-Optimal Early Stopping with Optimal Communication
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2553
Authors: Fatima Elsheimy, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Julian Loss, Charalampos Papamanthou
Summary: Minimizing both the round and communication complexity of Byzantine agreement (BA) is a longstanding problem. In the synchronous setting, early stopping protocols aim to terminate in number of rounds that is proportional to the actual number $f\leq t$ of corruptions in an execution, rather than on the worst case threshold $t$. The lower bound on the round complexity for such protocols is known to be $\min\{f+2, t+1\}$ rounds. Existing protocols, however, achieve either round complexity close to the optimal bound or low communication complexity, but not both simultaneously. Elsheimy, Loss, and Papamanthou (ASIACRYPT 2024) obtain $(1+\epsilon)f+O(1)$ rounds for any $1> \epsilon>0$, with $O(n^4f \kappa)$ communication. In contrast, Lenzen and Sheikholeslami (PODC 2022) achieve asymptotically optimal $O(n \cdot t)$ communication for $t3$, but with a $25f+13$ number of rounds.
In this work, we present deterministic synchronous Byzantine agreement protocols that achieve new tradeoffs between early stopping round complexity and communication. For $t3$, without cryptographic setup, we obtain $f+O(\sqrt{f\log f})$ termination rounds with optimal $O(n\cdot t)$ communication (here and throughout, $\sqrt{f}$ denotes $\sqrt{f+1}$ and $\log f$ denotes $\log(f+2)$, so that the bounds are well defined when $f=0$). Thus, our round complexity has the optimal leading coefficient of one, with a sublinear additive overhead. By allowing slightly higher communication, we reduce this overhead to $O(\sqrt f)$, obtaining $f+O(\sqrt f)$ rounds with $O(n\cdot t+f^2\log f)$ communication. Finally, for $t<n/2$, assuming a public key infrastructure and threshold signatures, we obtain $f+O(\sqrt f)$ rounds with $O(n\cdot t\cdot\kappa)$ bits of communication, where $\kappa$ is the signature length.

item.title: CHARRM - Characterizing Hardware Leakage in the Robust Random Probing Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2552
Authors: Armand Schinkel, Pascal Sasdrich
Summary: Masking is a prevalent countermeasure against passive physical implementation attacks such as Side-Channel Analysis (SCA). Despite its theoretical soundness, the practical application of masking is often fraught with complexity and prone to errors, underscoring the necessity for automated security verification. This paper presents a comprehensive methodology for efficient security verification in the $(g, t, c)$-robust $(p, \epsilon)$-random probing model. In particular, we advance the state-of-the-art concept of leakage characteristics to account for robust probe extension schemes across arbitrary circuit structures, enabling efficient leakage probability bound computation for glitch-extended and transition-extended robust probing scenarios. By further linking the leakage characteristic to the Set of Input Shares (SIS) function, we extend our verification methodology to established composability notions. Our automated reasoning framework demonstrates practicality and superior performance and accuracy for larger circuits in comparative evaluations with \ironmask as state-of-the-art competitor. For the first time, our method allows for the exact verification of larger, composed circuit structures, validated by corresponding case studies. Consequently, this work advances the state-of-the-art in automated hardware security verification, providing a versatile tool for evaluating the security of masked cryptographic implementations against SCA in the presence of transient physical effects.

item.title: Privacy with Leakage from Falsifiable Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2551
Authors: Francesco Berti, Itamar Levi
Summary: An inherent challenge in cryptography is finding realistic and meaningful models and assumptions. Such assumptions must be fal- sifiable. For symmetric-key cryptography in the standard model (i.e., black-box without leakage), it is conjectured that we have identified the right assumptions: pseudorandom functions and permutations (PRFs and PRPs). However, when considering side-channel attacks (SCAs) that exploit physical side-channel leakage, the answer is less clear. Moreover, the requirements for integrity and privacy may differ in the leakage-aware SCA setting. For integrity: due to advances in the so-called unbounded leakage model, it is sufficient to claim integrity based only on black-box properties by instantiating a single strongly unpredictable-with-leakage (tweakable) block cipher. For privacy: one approach relied on simulatabil- ity, proposed by Yu and Standaert at CRYPTO 2013. That is, it should be possible to simulate leakage traces without access to the underlying secret key. Unfortunately, simulating the leakage behavior of a complex electronic system and arguing that distinguishing simulation from reality is hard has proved highly challenging (e.g., Galea et al., ASIACRYPT 2014, and Deperz et al., Cascade 2026). In this paper, we propose a new model and assumption. We isolate a key component, namely the key-refreshing process, and provide a security definition for it that is both falsifiable in practice and usable in security proofs: secure refreshing. Like simulatability, this assumption is designed to capture the security of the key-refreshing process. Rather than re- lying on a simulator, however, we formalize security through a direct refreshing experiment that can be practically falsified by evaluation lab- oratories. Therefore, our approach avoids many of the concrete problems and challenges associated with previous models. Furthermore, inspired by this new assumption (and its accompanying model), and to provide an additional security assumption for the strongly SCA-protected leak- free component, we introduce strongly protected secure refreshing. As one concrete example, using these assumptions, we prove the privacy of the well-known PSV encryption scheme. We provide the first privacy proof based only on falsifiable assumptions and, importantly, without assuming that the strongly protected component is leak-free which can effectively translate to significant computational cost reduction.

item.title: PPGA: A Framework for Privacy-Preserving Graph Algorithms using the Prepare/Propagate/Gather/Apply Paradigm
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2550
Authors: Andreas Brüggemann, Simon Brunnauer, Thomas Schneider
Summary: Privacy-preserving graph computation enables the secure analysis of graphs modeling social interactions and networks, financial transactions, etc., while keeping the graph private. One approach is to use secure multiparty computation (MPC), allowing different clients to contribute parts of a graph without need of disclosure, and multiple MPC protocols have been proposed for running message-passing-based graph analysis. Yet, existing public implementations are prototypes for fixed analysis functions that require substantial MPC expertise to modify and extend. We present PPGA, a practical framework based on the MultiCent protocol (PETS'25). PPGA lets users define their custom message-passing graph algorithms with a high-level interface, clients input parts of the graph, and then runs the algorithm in MPC. It significantly improves performance compared to MultiCent's implementation, running BFS on a graph of size |V|+|E|=30 million in 23 minutes without leaking the graph topology.

item.title: Firebolt: Fast, Lightweight, Malicious Non-Interactive Vector-OLE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2549
Authors: Michael Adjedj, Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolaos Makriyannis
Summary: We introduce a new maliciously-secure vector oblivious linear evaluation (VOLE), building upon a recent construction of (semi-honest) Paillier-based non-interactive VOLE. Our protocol is non-interactive (the sender can adaptively reveal entries of the VOLE using a single message to the receiver) and enjoys low communication (535 bytes for each VOLE entry) and low computation (around 5ms per party, single-threaded). Our protocol can be used as a drop-in replacement for less efficient VOLEs used in a variety of threshold schemes. We exemplify it by devising a new concurrently-secure two-round two-party ECDSA protocol that significantly improves over the state of the art. Along the way, we introduce several new strategies for proving shortness of plaintexts in Paillier ciphertexts or integer commitments, and we devise a modular framework for building threshold-ECDSA in a VOLE-hybrid model with concurrent security without requiring the use of (typically less efficient) UC-secure VOLE. All of these contributions are of independent interest.

item.title: Evasive Inner Product Functional Encryption Is Broken Too
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2548
Authors: Shweta Agrawal, Anuja Modi, Anshu Yadav, Shota Yamada
Summary: We show that the Evasive Inner Product Functional Encryption assumption introduced by Hsieh, Lin and Luo (Eurocrypt 2024) is false in its full generality. Our counterexample adds to a long sequence of works that have attacked different variants of Evasive LWE, taking down another instance that has been considered ``public coin'' (and hence safe) in the literature.
Our attack extends the counterexample against pseudorandom functional encryption ($\mathsf{PRFE}$), developed by Agrawal, Modi, Yadav and Yamada (TCC 2025) to encompass the notion of Evasive Inner Product Functional Encryption ($\mathsf{evIPFE}$) proposed by Hsieh, Lin and Luo (Eurocrypt 2024). The original attack relied crucially on the underlying functional encryption scheme being powerful enough to compute pseudorandom functions; our attack shows, perhaps surprisingly, that the much weaker ``evasive'' inner product functionality suffices to mount the attack.
We interpret our attack as showing that even the slightest power given to the adversary in choosing unrestricted private coins in the evasive LWE family of assumptions, renders it insecure.

item.title: $\mathcal{iO}$ from LWE with Structured Preimage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2547
Authors: Shweta Agrawal, Anuja Modi, Anshu Yadav, Shota Yamada
Summary: Constructing $\mathcal{iO}$ from simple, safe assumptions in the post-quantum regime is an important problem with wide-ranging applications. In this work, we make progress towards this goal. We formulate a new, arguably simple assumption called LWE with Structured Preimage that suffices to build $\mathcal{iO}$. Our assumption is instance-independent, falsifiable and non-interactive. Our assumption posits that a set of LWE (Learning With Errors) samples is indistinguishable from random given a short Gaussian matrix which is carefully chosen to satisfy the required functionality while avoiding problematic leakage.
We provide a thorough cryptanalysis of our assumption, using the extensive cryptanalytic effort against the related evasive LWE assumption (Wee, Eurocrypt 2022 and Tsabary, Crypto 2022) to gain confidence. We emphasize that our assumption is superficially similar but fundamentally different from evasive LWE. Thus, we obtain $\mathcal{iO}$ from a simple lattice assumption whose hardness is somewhat better understood as compared to brand new assumptions.

item.title: New IND-CPA-D Attacks on BFV and BGV
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2546
Authors: Hyeongmin CHOE, Minsik Kang, Damien Stehlé
Summary: IND-CPA-D security is an extension of IND-CPA security introduced in the context of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). It captures the situation where the computation result is known to the adversary; it is in particular necessary for FHE with threshold decryption. This work presents three new attacks in this situation on the BFV and BGV FHE schemes, when their parameters are instantiated with heuristic assumptions commonly used to enable correctness.
We first extend the \emph{bootstrapping failure attacks} from Cheon \emph{et al.} [CCS'24] on the DM/CGGI and CKKS schemes, to both BFV and BGV. We focus on BGV when instantiated with the so-called powerful-basis representation of ring elements. The second attack relies on \emph{skewing the ciphertext noise} in BFV, making it outpace the heuristic noise bounds for plaintext-ciphertext multiplications. This is achieved by crafting plaintexts, for which the noise bounds do not hold. The third and last attack focuses on outpacing the noise growth in BFV ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications. For this purpose, we \emph{skew the mask} part of the ciphertext by selecting a random encryption of zero, whose addition yields a ciphertext with a sufficiently large mask norm. While the first two attacks successfully recover the secret key, the last attack instead breaks the IND-CPA-D indistinguishability game.
We report experiments on all these attacks, based on the HElib and OpenFHE libraries, respectively, for BGV and BFV. Notably, the second attack implemented in OpenFHE fully recovers the secret key in a few minutes to a few hours, depending on the parameters.

item.title: A Note on the Security of ECDSA with Presignatures or Biased Nonces
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2545
Authors: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolaos Makriyannis
Summary: Over the years, several ECDSA security experiments have been proposed to enable faster distributed ECDSA signing. These experiments are not known to reduce to the standard ECDSA game, and recent work (Groth and Shoup, Eurocrypt 2022) shows that some are vulnerable, especially when combined with raw signing (signing hash digests directly, rather than pre-hashed messages) and additive key derivation. Furthermore, several of these variants are implemented in public libraries and used by companies, sometimes in commercially deployed products, yet lack sound security foundations.
In this note, we revisit the security landscape of these alternative modes of operation for ECDSA. As our main result, we show that the security of some of these variants, which are used in the wild, is equivalent in the generic group and random oracle model to a standard conjecture from fine-grained complexity on the average-case hardness of the $k$-SUM problem. We complement our study by proving lower bounds, conditioned on fine-grained complexity conjectures, on the running time of generic group model attacks against other standard modes of operation analyzed in (Groth and Shoup, Eurocrypt 2022). Overall, our results provide a complete picture of the security landscape of ECDSA variants, and reveal an elegant connection with (old and new) conjectures from the field of fine-grained complexity.

item.title: Blind-DLPA: An End-to-End Framework for Profiled Blind Side-Channel Analysis
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2544
Authors: Pei Cao, Chi Zhang, Dawu Gu
Summary: Conventional profiled side-channel analysis generally assumes that the plaintexts or ciphertexts associated with target traces are available during key recovery. We consider a profiled blind setting in which the attacker can obtain labeled traces from a profiling device using known inputs and keys, but observes only leakage traces from the target device. Under this setting, we propose Blind-DLPA, an end-to-end multi-task framework for {profiled blind side-channel analysis (profiled BSCA) that processes complete preprocessed trace windows} and jointly estimates the soft Hamming-weight posteriors of an input variable and a key-dependent intermediate variable. These posteriors are combined with pre-computed theoretical joint distributions to rank the key hypotheses, avoiding both manual {point of interest} (PoI) selection and a parameter-sensitive Gaussian label-error model. Evaluations on unprotected AES and Kyber demonstrate successful key recovery, while experiments on protected AES implementations show robustness to desynchronization and Boolean masking. To the best of our knowledge, Blind-DLPA provides the first reported profiled blind key recovery on the ASCAD dataset, reaching a guessing entropy of zero with 39 attack traces. Complementing these results, we revisit the Ascon Hamming-weight joint-distribution model adopted in prior work and identify previously overlooked collisions between key-dependent theoretical distributions that prevent unique key recovery under this model.

item.title: A Key-Recovery Attack on the GTLN Knapsack Cryptosystem via Continued Fractions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2543
Authors: Shiyi zhou, Yingpu Deng, Shi Ying
Summary: We present a continued-fraction key-recovery attack on the knapsack-based public-key cryptosystem proposed by Gómez-Torrecillas, Lobillo, and Navarro (GTLN). The key observation is that ratios of public-key differences closely approximate rational numbers with small denominators, enabling their exact recovery by continued fractions. Divisibility relations in the recovered fractions yield multiples of two private-key integers through greatest common divisor computations. Once these two integers are identified by a bounded cofactor search, all remaining private-key integers except the modulus and the shift are uniquely determined. Further greatest common divisor computations, cofactor enumeration, and modular inversion then recover the secret modulus and shift. The above process of key recovery uses only public keys. For fixed cofactor bounds, the algorithm runs in polynomial time in the public-key bit length, while a heuristic analysis predicts a high probability of recovering the original key. In experiments with prime-based key generation, our Python implementation recovered the complete private key in all 2,400 trials across the 24 recommended parameter sets, with each attack taking less than 0.05 seconds.

item.title: From if to Oops: Turning a conditional into a key-recovery oracle
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2542
Authors: Gustavo Banegas, Nia Dimitrova, Monika Trimoska
Summary: Deterministic variants of CSIDH remove randomness from the group action, either through implementation techniques or, as in Houben's deterministic CSIDH and OSIDH-LD, by design. Since earlier fault attacks on CSIDH mostly target random point sampling, determinism seems to close that avenue. We show that it opens another: every secret-dependent step occurs at a fixed, public point of every execution, so an attacker can fault the same step repeatedly. Our attack forces the mask that selects which of two lanes computes the next isogeny to zero, for example by skipping one instruction. Whether the output changes reveals whether a secret exponent reaches a chosen threshold, and a binary search over these thresholds recovers the full key with one fault per execution: at most 297 oracle queries for OSIDH-LD and 222 for deterministic CSIDH with CSIDH-512-sized keys. We recover full OSIDH-LD keys in a software fault simulation of the reference implementation, and show on a ChipWhisperer-Lite that the targeted instruction is skipped with probability at least $0.94$ at an isolated fault position. Finally, we argue that fault resistance requires giving up determinism, and propose countermeasures relying on randomization.

item.title: Provable Lattice Reduction in Nearly the Time of QR Factorization
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2541
Authors: Yang Zhou, Zhedong Wang, Mingsheng Wang
Summary: We propose a deterministic lattice-reduction algorithm with bit complexity matching QR factorization up to logarithmic factors, and an implementation that uses fewer instructions than \texttt{flatter} (CRYPTO 2023) in our benchmarks. The key technical innovations are iterative precision management, a finer-grained potential analysis, and a new representation for bases and transformations, all integrated into a recursive framework. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of our algorithm, and show that, for fixed reduction and output accuracy, the running time is $\widetilde O\!\left( n^\omega\bigl(1+\log\kappa_{\rm col}(\mathbf B)\bigr)\right)$, where $\mathbf B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}$ is a nonsingular lattice basis and $\kappa_{\rm col}$ is the optimally column-scaled spectral condition number. This gives a finer complexity than prior art, by allowing a tighter condition number $\kappa_{\rm col}$. Besides, through a new observation on the recursive structure, we demonstrate that the algorithm is free from heuristic assumptions. We compare our implementation with \texttt{flatter} on q-ary, NTRU-like, scaled q-ary, and Coppersmith inputs. Our implementation uses fewer instructions in all 153 executions. The median ratios of \texttt{flatter}'s instruction count to ours are 1.55 for ordinary q-ary inputs and 1.86 for NTRU-like inputs.

item.title: Efficient and Compact High-order Masking Raccoon on Memory Constrained Devices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2540
Authors: Junhao Huang, Yiteng Sun, Jipeng Zhang, Weijia Wang, Donglong Chen, Haiyang Xue, Guomin Yang
Summary: Raccoon, presented at CRYPTO 2024, is a provably secure lattice-based signature scheme featuring an $O(d \log{d})$ masking overhead. Although it did not advance beyond the first-round of NIST's additional call for post-quantum digital signatures, Raccoon remains a promising candidate due to its low masking overhead and strong provable side-channel resistance.
This paper proposes the first efficient and compact implementation of high-order Raccoon on the ARM Cortex-M4, with a focus on optimizing its polynomial multiplication, sampling, and memory consumption. 1) For polynomial multiplication, we present a consecutive 32-bit NTT/INTT implementation for the two moduli in Raccoon, enabling optimal 3+3+3 layer merging to reduce memory-access overhead, together with extensive lazy reduction to minimize modular reductions. As a side contribution, we propose a novel negative double Montgomery reduction technique to accelerate double modular reductions in multi-moduli NTT. 2) For polynomial sampling, we identify and resolve a previously overlooked performance bottleneck caused by frequent incremental SHAKE256 invocations for small data chunks on ARM Cortex-M4. By transitioning to the one-shot approach, we achieve speedups of at least $1.80\times$ across all sampling routines in Raccoon. 3) Finally, we explore memory-saving techniques to enable the practical deployment of high-order masked Raccoon (up to 32 orders) on resource-constrained IoT devices.
The proposed implementations outperform the Raccoon reference implementation by $1.85\times$-$2.25\times$. Notably, high-order masked Raccoon-192 outperforms masked Dilithium3 by $3.12\times, 8.07\times$, and $2.71\times$ at masking orders $d=2$, $4$, and $8$, respectively. Finally, the leakage evaluations confirm that the second-order Raccoon implementation provides strong resistance to differential power analysis (DPA) once micro-architectural transitional leakages are mitigated.

item.title: Implementing Predicate Encryption for Branching Programs: Private Computation over Key-Homomorphic Encodings Without FHE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2539
Authors: Sora Suegami
Summary: Predicate encryption (PE) encrypts a message under an attribute that the ciphertext hides, allowing a secret key for a predicate to recover the message only when the attribute satisfies the predicate. Existing public-key implementations support useful specialized predicates, but enforcing heterogeneous conditions with one key requires an attribute representation fixed before encryption, which grows with the supported types of conditions and cannot express types it does not anticipate, such as regular expressions. Lattice-based PE for general circuits is far more expressive, but existing constructions rely on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), typically evaluated as a Boolean circuit over key-homomorphic encodings, which expands the computation and amplifies noise growth and leads to impractically large parameters. Existing PE thus offers either practicality for restricted predicates or expressiveness at an impractical cost.
We present a lattice-based PE scheme for branching programs that avoids FHE entirely and combines heterogeneous conditions in a single predicate over a common attribute representation. It rests on two techniques: asymmetric multiplication, which multiplies a hidden program state by an encrypted attribute symbol through decryption inside an encoding, and lookup tables over exponents, which evaluate arbitrary state transitions on a single encoding by ring automorphisms. Under circular Ring-LWE, the scheme is selectively weakly attribute-hiding against polynomially many colluding unauthorized keys.
We give, to our knowledge, the first implementation of PE for a predicate class as expressive as branching programs. On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, for a predicate that combines a range check and a regular-expression check on a $10$-bit attribute, with parameters targeting $128$-bit security against known Ring-LWE attacks, encryption takes $4.06$ hours, key generation $4.70$ hours, and decryption $4.23$ hours, with $342.25$ GB ciphertexts. These costs remain large, but compared with a single FHE multiplication evaluated as a Boolean circuit over encodings, the basic step of PE that evaluates FHE over encodings, whose ciphertexts alone occupy tens of exabytes per attribute bit, our ciphertexts are at least $2\times10^9$ times smaller per attribute bit, and our decryption needs at least $2\times10^{16}$ times fewer $64$-bit integer multiplications.

item.title: Optimizing HQC with Enhanced Parallel Binary Polynomial Multiplication on GPUs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2538
Authors: DongCheon Kim, JunHyeok Choi, Wai Kong Lee, Seog Chung Seo
Summary: Graphics processing units (GPUs) are widely employed as accelerators in modern servers to handle key-establishment requests in bulk. Such deployments require the GPU implementation to sustain high throughput while keeping each request within its latency bound. In this work, we present a high-performance, end-to-end GPU implementation of Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC), a code-based key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). We propose two novel techniques to accelerate the dominant cost of HQC, which is binary polynomial multiplication over Galois Field GF(2). The first is a parallelization of the Frobenius additive fast Fourier transform (FAFFT), and the second is a mapping of the cyclic product, viewed as a Toeplitz matrix–vector product, onto one-bit integer (INT1) tensor cores. We further explore the design space of these multipliers, measuring them directly on the GPU to derive the best combination for the architecture. We further propose a GPU-resident computation strategy that keeps the entire KEM on the GPU, thereby reducing costly memory traffic. Beyond multiplication, we introduce warp-level parallelization strategies to accelerate the remaining stages, hashing, Reed–Muller/Reed–Solomon (RM/RS) coding, and fixed-weight sampling, which become the performance bottleneck once multiplication is optimized. By varying the mapping of KEM instances to GPU threads, we derive five variants spanning the trade-off between throughput and latency and organize them into a thread-to-KEM mapping taxonomy. On an RTX 4090, the Coarse-Grained (CG) variant maximizes batch throughput. Our multiplier reaches 3,828k polymul/s for standalone multiplication, about 2.9× the latest GPU HQC implementation HIGH, and for the full KEM the CG variant achieves 1.56×, 1.55×, and 2.03× higher end-to-end throughput than HIGH for keygen, encaps, and decaps. For single-shot latency the tensor-core-based BMMAw variant achieves a latency as low as 254 µs. The proposed warp-parallel FGmw variant still attains a latency of 354 µs, demonstrating that our approach remains effective on GPU architectures lacking INT1 tensor-core support. All five variants are further evaluated on an RTX 3090 and an embedded Jetson AGX Orin to confirm cross-platform portability.

item.title: SAT and Neural Network Filters for Misinjections in Fault Attacks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2537
Authors: Hanbeom Shin, Dongwoo Kang, Donggeun Kwon, Seokhie Hong, HeeSeok Kim
Summary: A misinjection, an injection that misses the fault form an attack assumes, can make an elimination fault attack discard the correct key. They occur when the attacker has not determined the timing of the device, and a random-delay countermeasure wider than the S-box layer can force them even on one who has. This paper presents a SAT filter that removes misinjections without the secret key, one injection at a time. It models the differential propagation from the injected round to the end of the cipher in SAT and rejects an injection when the model has no solution for the assumed fault and the observed ciphertext difference. The paper also presents a neural network filter, which passes an injection when the score of a network trained for the same decision is at least 0.5, and a combined filter, which passes it only when the SAT model of the injection also has a solution. We measure the filters on faults injected by clock glitching into GIFT-64, GIFT-128 and BAKSHEESH on a microcontroller, in three settings, a non-profiling attacker without and with a random-delay countermeasure and a profiling attacker with it. The SAT filter rejected none of the 14669 intended faults and, for the non-profiling attacker without the random-delay countermeasure, at least 0.940 of the misinjections at the full-diffusion round, over at least 385 each. For the same attacker it raises the success probability of ToFA on BAKSHEESH, which recovers the master key, from 5.2% to 61.2%, and the combined filter raises it to 96.2%, each over 2000 trials.

item.title: IISFA: Ineffective Instruction-Skip Fault Attacks on Bitslice Implementations
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2536
Authors: Hanbeom Shin, Dongwoo Kang, Donggeun Kwon, Seokhie Hong, HeeSeok Kim
Summary: Redundancy countermeasures prevent differential fault analysis by withholding faulty ciphertexts. Ineffective fault analysis and statistical ineffective fault attacks exploit executions in which an injected fault leaves the result unchanged, using constraints on intermediate values or statistical bias to recover keys. In this paper, we present an Ineffective Instruction-Skip Fault Attack (IISFA) on bitsliced implementations protected by redundancy. A bitsliced instruction processes $m$ S-boxes simultaneously. Skipping it leaves the group unchanged exactly when all $m$ S-box inputs belong to its ineffective set, which we compute from the implementation. Each ciphertext output by the device therefore restricts all $m$ $n$-bit subkeys to candidates whose S-box inputs belong to that set. The ineffective probability specifies how often a uniformly random S-box input makes the skip ineffective, and its $m$-th power gives the ciphertext output probability for independent inputs. We determine which key candidates remain indistinguishable under a single target instruction. We give key-recovery procedures for both known and chosen plaintexts and combine different target instructions across queries, with one instruction skipped per execution. We calculate expected injection counts or enclosing intervals for the known- and chosen-plaintext procedures from the ineffective sets and use them to reduce the search for efficient target sequences. We evaluate five bitsliced implementations of GIFT, SKINNY and PIPO on an 8-bit AVR microcontroller under a redundancy countermeasure using clock glitches. All measured key-recovery campaigns succeed in every trial.

item.title: Quantum State Search with Classical Interactive Advice
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2535
Authors: MOHAMMED BARHOUSH
Summary: We study whether a quantum verifier can find a hidden quantum state by exchanging classical messages with an unbounded prover who knows the state. The verifier has access to a reflection oracle about the target. For a Haar-random $n$-qubit target, we prove that achieving constant average fidelity with the target requires $(q+1)^2(B+1)=\Omega(2^n)$, where $q$ is the number of verifier queries and $B$ is the total prover-to-verifier communication. The bound allows arbitrary classical interaction and unrestricted computation between queries. Our proof extends the lower bound of Aaronson and Kuperberg from a single classical proof to an arbitrary classical interaction.
As a result, we obtain a quantum-oracle separation of UniqueQMA from QCIP with polynomially many classical messages. In particular, we give a unitary oracle $\mathcal{U}$ such that there exists a language $L\in\mathrm{UniqueQMA}^{\mathcal{U}}$ but $L\notin\mathrm{QCIP}^{\mathcal{U}}$.
We further give an oracle construction for a notion known as QMA-QCIP[2] gap problem. This gives average case hardness for a QMA language under classical access to a QCIP[2] decision oracle and is used in establishing negative results on witness encryption and quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.

item.title: Circular Dragon: $\widetilde{{O}}$ptimal Adaptively Secure Distributed Randomness/Key Generation and Parallel Broadcast
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2534
Authors: Hanwen Feng, Yuan Lu, Tiancheng Mai, Qiang Tang
Summary: We present the first strongly adaptive common coin protocol, under the PKI setup (in the random oracle model and the algebraic group model, yet with no trusted dealer), that (i) achieves the optimal resilience $t< n/2$ in synchronous networks, and (ii) attains near-optimal asymptotics: near-quadratic communication $O(\kappa \lambda n^2\log n)$ and logarithmic rounds $O(\kappa\log n)$, with failure probability $\textsf{negl}(\lambda)+2^{-\kappa}$, where $\lambda$ (resp. $\kappa$) is the computational (resp. statistical) security parameter. Furthermore, the coin protocol assumes no memory erasure. At its core is a ``special-purpose'' distributed key generation (DKG) protocol that produces a secret in an elliptic-curve group. Our common coin immediately implies the first strongly adaptive and optimally resilient Byzantine Agreement with subcubic communication and sublinear rounds in the absence of a trusted dealer. Furthermore, we give two non-trivial applications of independent interest: (i) a strongly adaptive Parallel Broadcast (PBC) under standard PKI with near-quadratic communication and logarithmic rounds, whereas all existing subcubic solutions (Gelles et al. CRYPTO'25, Civit et al. PODC'24) require at least linear rounds; (ii) a strongly adaptive ``general-purpose'' DKG for field-element secrets with $O(\lambda\kappa n^2\log n)$ communication and $O(\kappa\log n)$ rounds (assuming memory erasures), fully compatible with legacy threshold schemes (BLS, Schnorr, ElGamal), improving upon (Feng et al. PODC'24), which requires $O(\lambda\kappa n^{2.5} \log n)$ communication and $O(n)$ rounds. Our core is a new design methodology, which we call \emph{Circular Dragon}. This extends the Dragon method (PODC'24) that was originally developed for sub-cubic communication DKG protocols but with linear rounds, by further reducing the round complexity.

item.title: Off-Key: Inconsistent MAC Keys Compromise Privacy in SPDZ-Family MPC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2533
Authors: Marcel Keller, Sela Navot, Nirvan Tyagi
Summary: SPDZ-family protocols for maliciously secure multi-party computation protect secret-shared values with message authentication codes (MACs) under a secret-shared global key. Their security requires that all values and preprocessing used together be authenticated under the same key. We present Off-Key, a privacy attack that exploits violations of this requirement. Depending on which specific MAC check protocol is used, a corrupted party can either recover the value of a shared secret from a single authentication check or test a guess through selective failure by modifying a MAC share and observing whether a masked check succeeds. While this attack does not compromise the theoretical security guarantees of the protocols, we demonstrate this key-consistency vulnerability in evaluated versions of MP-SPDZ, SCALE-MAMBA, and FANNG-MPC, which allow a corrupted party to use different keys across batches, threads, or process runs. To help implementations avoid this class of attacks, we identify the state that enforces key consistency in representative preprocessing protocols and show how preserving and reusing it prevents the attack.

item.title: HERMES: High-Performance Private Decoding for Large Language Models
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2532
Authors: MohammadHossein Olyaiy, Cora Shao, Dingqing Yang, Mohammad Shahrad, Mieszko Lis
Summary: Privacy-preserving inference (PI) enables users to query large language models (LLMs) without revealing their prompts, but incurs substantial computation and communication overhead. Prior PI systems primarily optimize prefill and time to first token (TTFT). This suits applications that need only a single output token, yet most real-world use cases require multi-token responses. Such autoregressive workloads are dominated by time per output token (TPOT) instead.
For the first time, we investigate generating full multi-token answers for real prompts under PI. We show that PI decode is hindered by two bottlenecks: (i) nonlinear kernels that require many interactive communication rounds, and (ii) attention protocols that underutilize ciphertext capacity and repeatedly re-encrypt or transmit the growing key and value (KV) cache.
We present HERMES, a PI system optimized for LLM decoding. HERMES replaces high-round nonlinear protocols with compute- and bandwidth-intensive alternatives that require fewer communication rounds. It also introduces a novel matrix-multiplication protocol based on homomorphic encryption that keeps the KV cache encrypted on the server and uses grouped-query attention (GQA) to improve ciphertext utilization. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, across the network conditions and prompts used in our evaluation, HERMES lowers TPOT by up to 2.7× and total PI latency by up to 2.1×.

item.title: High-Precision CKKS with Focal Units
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2531
Authors: Jung Hee Cheon, Junho Lee
Summary: In CKKS, higher precision requires a larger scaling factor, increasing modulus consumption during homomorphic arithmetic and leaving less modulus available after bootstrapping under the same modulus budget. We introduce Focused CKKS, which trades unused SIMD slots for precision through focused rescaling and key-switching based on cyclotomic units. These units reduce error in selected focus slots while allowing larger error in the background slots. Using only a $1/k$ fraction of the slots provides approximately $k$ times as many bits of precision at the same scaling factor and CKKS parameter setting. Such a high-precision multiplication costs the same as an ordinary CKKS multiplication, with each focus slot supported by $(k-1)$ background slots. More generally, the construction supports different precision requirements across slots.
We also construct a bootstrapping procedure tailored to Focused CKKS. Only the base modulus at the bottom level needs to grow with the target precision; the remaining bootstrapping computation maintains approximately the same modulus consumption by using fewer slots. By adapting the high-precision bootstrapping based on discrete CKKS and performing its error-cleaning step in Focused CKKS, we further reduce this base modulus by approximately the same factor $k$.

item.title: Computing endomorphisms of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces in time and memory \(p^{4/5+o(1)}\)
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2530
Authors: Marc Houben, Lam L. Pham
Summary: We present an algorithm for computing endomorphisms of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces over finite fields. Under a standard heuristic, we obtain a non-scalar polarized endomorphism in expected time and memory $p^{4/5 + o(1)}$.

item.title: The Covering Radius of $\text{RM}(1,9)$ is Precisely $242$
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2529
Authors: Xiang-dong Hou, Evelyn Sabo, Freeman Slaughter
Summary: Let $\text{RM}(r,n)$ be the $r$th order Reed-Muller code of length $2^n$, and let $\rho(r,n)$ denote its covering radius, so that $\rho(1,n)$ is the largest possible nonlinearity of a Boolean function in $n$ variables. For odd $n$, the value of $\rho(1,n)$ was previously known only for $n\le 7$. It is known that $242\le\rho(1,9)\le 244$, but the exact determination of $\rho(1,9)$ has been a long-standing open question. We give a computer-assisted proof that $\rho(1,9)=242$. We first show that a function of nonlinearity $243$ would yield one of nonlinearity $244$, so it suffices to exclude $244$. Divisibility properties of the Walsh spectrum then attach to any function of nonlinearity $244$ a cubic $p$ whose spectrum attains the sharp bound $\sum\limits_a|W_p(a)|\le 10240$, and the cases of equality take one of two forms. One form is eliminated directly. The other is eliminated by an exhaustive computation that leverages the classification of the $349$ orbits in $\text{RM}(3,9)/\text{RM}(2,9)$ under $\text{GL}(9,2)$, using Langevin's catalog of representatives together with an audit of its completeness, and the enumeration is carried out twice with independent implementations. The notebook to verify the computer search portion, $\texttt{Verify_RM(1,9).ipynb}$, contains all data and recomputes each check, and may be found in the repository $\texttt{https://github.com/FreemanSlaughter/Covering-Radius}$.

item.title: Revisiting the Security of VDOO
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2528
Authors: Siyu Li, Hao Guo, Peigen Li, Siyong Tao
Summary: VDOO is a multivariate signature scheme submitted to the Next-generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms Program (NGCC). We study the security of its submitted parameter sets. In this paper, VDOO is described as a multilayer Rainbow construction. By retaining only its last oil space, we obtain a generalized UOV instance and apply existing wedge attacks.
For the parameter set targeting 512-bit security, we estimate costs of $2^{432}$ and $2^{379}$ gates for the reconciliation and intersection variants, respectively. These estimates rely on the assumptions of the attack model and are below both the claimed security level and the attack costs reported in the specification.
Our analysis uses only the generalized UOV structure. The additional information in the multilayer structure may allow further improvements. Our results also motivate further study of parameter choices that balance resistance to known attacks with signing efficiency.

item.title: How Secure are NTRU+ Keys? Analysing the Best Module Attacks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2527
Authors: Paola de Perthuis, Filip Trenkić
Summary: A recent analysis of module-BKZ [Ducas–Engleberts–Perthuis, Asiacrypt'25] predicts subexponential speedups for lattice reduction on module lattices over cyclotomic fields whose conductor has small odd prime factors. This threatens NTRU+, the South Korean standard for key encapsulation, and related schemes; however, the short vectors one seeks to find are short in the coefficient geometry, whereas module-BKZ operates in the canonical geometry.
We introduce relative canonical and relative coefficient embeddings, realising a module over a cyclotomic field $K$ as a module over any subfield $L$, and characterise when the two agree up to scaling: exactly when the radicals of their respective conductors $c$ and $\ell$ satisfy $\mathrm{rad}(c)/\mathrm{rad}(\ell) \in \{1,2\}$. Furthermore we quantify the distortion incurred in general when passing between embeddings, and hence identify the optimal subfield for module-BKZ and BKZ to use.
Estimating the cost of the best attack with simulation-based models [Perthuis–Trenkić, PQCrypto'26], we find that the best module attack saves only 4–10 blocksizes, costing NTRU+ keys at most three bits of security in the Core-SVP model.
