Conceptually, we propose architectural changes to general-purpose processors at the Register-Transfer Level (RTL) that remove the root causes of micro-architectural leakages. The application of these changes enables the secure execution of masked software without introducing micro-architectural leakage under the Robust but Relaxed (RR) d-probing model, thereby removing the need for complex, security-aware compilers and hardware-specific workarounds in the software. While our countermeasures can be applied to many micro-architectures, we formally prove the security of each countermeasure individually and integrate them into the Ibex processor, whose security we evaluate as a whole through tool-assisted leakage assessment of the full netlist and physical experiments on a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA).

item.title: Secret Sharing from Non-Extractable Randomness
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2477
Authors: Divesh Aggarwal
Summary: Bosley and Dodis (TCC 2007) proved that a class of imperfect randomness sources that suffices for information-theoretic encryption of messages longer than the logarithm of the key length must admit deterministic extraction of nearly uniform bits, and asked whether the same is true of two-out-of-two secret sharing. Aggarwal, Chung, Obremski, and Ribeiro (TCC 2022) gave a positive answer for schemes that are in addition leakage-resilient or non-malleable; the original question remained open.
We answer it in the negative. For every $b\ge2$ we construct a class of flat sources on $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$, each of min-entropy at least $b$, together with a perfectly correct and perfectly private two-out-of-two scheme that shares a $b$-bit secret into two $(b+1)$-bit shares using any source in the class, and we show that every deterministic map from $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$ to $\{0,1\}$ is at statistical distance at least $1/6$ from uniform on some source in the class. This implies that sharing a long enough secret does not require extractable randomness. The proof is a short parity argument. The idea of the construction extends to other thresholds: for two-out-of-$n$ and $r$-out-of-$r$ sharing we give perfect schemes with $(b+1)$-bit shares, private for classes of flat sources from which no single bit can be extracted with error below $1/(4n-2)$ and $1/(2(2^r-1))$, respectively.

item.title: On the Hardness of Finding Permutation Automorphisms of Linear Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2476
Authors: Michele Battagliola, Giuseppe D'Alconzo, Laura Mattiuz, Paolo Santini, Federica Zanetti
Summary: We study the hardness of finding permutation automorphisms of linear codes. We look into three main problems: $\mathsf{AUT}$, $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ which, respectively, ask to find a non-trivial automorphism, a generating set and the order of the automorphism group. We give polynomial time reductions from $\mathsf{AUT}$ to $\mathsf{ISO}$ (the problem of finding a permutation isomorphism between two linear codes), and from $\mathsf{ISO}$ to $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$. This shows that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ are unlikely to be easy in the worst case, since all known solvers for $\mathsf{ISO}$ take exponential time if the hull dimension (the subspace given by the intersection between the code and its dual) is large enough. Furthermore, we give a reduction from $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ to the problem of finding generators for the automorphism group of a graph, which we refer to as $\mathsf{GraphAUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$. Up to some polynomial factors, the reduction runs in time $O(n^{h})$, with $n$ being the code length and $h$ the hull dimension: for $h = O\big(\log(n)\big)$, this implies that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ can be solved in worst case quasi-polynomial time. We also give a simpler version of the reduction, running in time which is exponential in the worst case (arguably, only for rather contrived codes), even for small $h$. However, heuristically, the algorithm is on average extremely efficient for small $h$. We use it as a concrete solver and show that a proof-of-concept implementation is significantly faster than the built-in implementations of Leon's and Feulner's algorithms provided by $\texttt{Magma}$ and $\texttt{Sagemath}$.

item.title: Tamper Sensing Meshes in Payment Terminals and Beyond
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2475
Authors: Jan Sebastian Götte, Björn Scheuermann
Summary: Card Payment Terminals commonly use tamper sensing meshes to deter physical attacks on devices handling sensitive data such as cryptographic keys. Although their use of such meshes is frequently referenced in research literature, the public record contains little research on their construction. Addressing this gap, in this paper we present the first comprehensive analysis of the practical implementation of tamper sensing meshes across a wide range of payment terminals, and some other devices such as ATM key pads and a data center HSM. We provide detailed photos of critical features. Based on our observations, we construct a taxonomy of mesh construction techniques. Our analysis reveals that most commercial devices use surprisingly simple construction techniques, and their structure size rarely approaches manufacturing limits.
Based on our analysis, we identify a concise set of design patterns for the construction of secure tamper sensing meshes. We conclude that designing tamper sensing meshes that exceed the industrial state of the art is viable even using inexpensive and easily available manufacturing processes. Our set of design recommendations creates a foundation for both the practical tamper sensing mesh implementations and for future research into their design. Our results enable researchers to base test specimens on concrete evidence of industrial practice.

item.title: Software-Pipelining The Number Theoretic Transform on Neural Processing Units: A Loop-Fission Methodology
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2474
Authors: Henri Vermeersch, Xander Pottier, Quinten Norga, Thomas de Ruijter, Ingrid Verbauwhede
Summary: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) rely heavily on the number theoretic transform (NTT) for efficient polynomial multiplication. While GPUs and FPGAs have been widely explored for NTT acceleration, neural processing units (NPUs), a rapidly growing class of AI accelerators, remain largely unexplored for cryptographic workloads. In this work, we develop a methodology for accelerating the NTT on NPUs, using AMD’s AI Engine (AIE) architecture as a representative NPU to develop and benchmark it. At its core is manual loop fission, in which large and complex loops are split into smaller primitives, enabling highly efficient software pipelining and avoiding memory stalls or register spilling. Applying it, we develop efficient Barrett reduction primitives and use these to construct three high-throughput, low-latency NTT implementations (radix-2, radix-4, and radix-8), achieving significant performance gains over the AIE compiler and prior literature. On AMD’s first-generation AIE specifically, we achieve speedups of $8.27\times$ to $13.2\times$ in throughput and $2.44\times$ to $10.3\times$ in latency per AIE tile in comparison with prior work. Our implementations support arbitrary NTT-friendly moduli and polynomial sizes up to degree 4096 for 14-bit moduli and 2048 for 30-bit moduli. Finally, we discuss the portability of our techniques to other NPU architectures, and identify which architectural features are most beneficial for NTT acceleration.

item.title: edaBits in the Exponent (edaBitE) and Issuer-Hiding Blind Signatures from ML-DSA and VOLE-in-the-Head
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2473
Authors: Carsten Baum, Marvin Beckmann
Summary: Blind signatures let a user obtain a signature by interacting with an issuer that controls the signing key, while the issuer never sees the message. They form the basis of anonymous credentials, which are the centerpiece of privacy-preserving digital identification to be deployed widely in the coming years. Existing plausibly quantum-secure blind signatures rely on bespoke cryptographic constructions, instead of standardized ones. This is dissatisfying from a cryptographic perspective, and also leads to practical issues: secret signing keys are often stored in secure elements, in which case only signature algorithms supported by certified secure elements can be the basis for deployed protocols.
We give the first blind signature whose issuer runs a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme unmodified. Issuance is just an ML-DSA signature on a commitment, and the blind signature is a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge, using the VOLE-in-the-head zero-knowledge proof system, of the ML-DSA signature. Security reduces to the EUF-CMA security of ML-DSA and to the proof system, with no new assumptions. A blind signature is about $1$ MB and takes under a second to produce and half a second to verify. Issuer-hiding and selective disclosure of signed attributes can easily be added on top for a few tens of kilobytes, at a proof size essentially independent of how many issuers the list names.
Underlying the construction is edaBitE, a novel batch consistency check between binary and prime-field commitments. In a non-interactive proof, the existing edaBits checks it replaces would be the single largest item in the blind signature. We believe that edaBitE is of independent interest.
